questions.q: Per this lesson, what specific question does a Change Advisory Board (CAB) exist to answer?
options: Whether a proposed approach fits the org's long-term architecture
Whether it's safe to make this specific change, at this specific time, in this specific way
Whether a developer wrote clean code
Whether the organization should adopt Salesforce at all
questions.explain: A CAB's job is narrower than general architecture review -- it evaluates the safety of deploying a specific, already-designed change at a specific time, not whether the underlying idea is architecturally sound.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a CAB should include representatives from affected business units, not just technical staff?
options: Business representatives are required by Salesforce licensing terms
Business representatives replace the need for a release or change manager
Technical staff are not allowed to vote on CAB decisions
A change that looks safe from a purely technical standpoint can still have an operational business-process consequence that only someone from the affected business unit would catch
questions.explain: The mix of perspectives on a CAB exists specifically so a change doesn't get approved by people who only see one slice of its impact -- a technically clean change can still break a business process.

questions.q: What is an ECAB, as described in this lesson?
options: A smaller, faster-acting subset of the CAB empowered to approve emergency changes outside the normal meeting cadence
A board that only reviews emergency changes after they've already been deployed, with no approval authority
An entirely separate body that has nothing to do with the regular CAB
A Salesforce Setup feature that automatically approves urgent changes
questions.explain: An ECAB is a small group with authority to approve on short notice, so urgent incidents don't have to wait for the regular scheduled CAB meeting -- but emergency changes still get a full after-the-fact review later.

questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish a CAB from an architecture review board (ARB)?
options: They are two names for the exact same body with no real difference
An ARB only reviews emergency changes, while a CAB only reviews standard changes
A CAB asks whether an already-designed change is safe to deploy now; an ARB asks, earlier and at design time, whether the proposed approach actually fits the org's architecture and standards
A CAB exists only for Apex code changes, while an ARB exists only for declarative changes
questions.explain: The CAB is a deployment-time safety review of a specific change; the ARB is a design-time review of whether the underlying approach fits the architecture, typically happening earlier and only for structurally significant changes.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does reviewing every single change with the same depth turn a CAB into a bottleneck?
options: Because low-risk changes like a new picklist value get the same lengthy review as high-risk changes, instead of being handled through a faster, pre-approved path
Because CABs are legally required to meet for at least three hours every time
Because bottlenecks only happen when no CAB exists at all
Because a CAB can only review one change per calendar year
questions.explain: Without the standard/normal/emergency risk tiering from Lesson 4, a CAB that gives every change equal scrutiny spends its limited time on low-risk work instead of the decisions that actually need a full review.
